newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe warns on power-sharing in last campaign lap.
newsitem.headline: Juppe warns on power-sharing in last campaign lap.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe warned on the last campaigning day on Friday that a left-wing win in parliamentary elections would cripple France because of unavoidable "cohabitation" or power-sharing.

In an interview with the newspaper Le Figaro, Juppe said the centre-right's priorities if it stays in power after the May 25-June 1 poll would include limiting the number of offices politicians can hold and giving women a bigger say.

"Experience shows that cohabitation does not put France in a strong position, it does not allow it to play its role to the full, chiefly on the European or international stage, and it puts a brake on or paralyses big economic decisions," he said.

Opinion polls released before last weekend's blackout suggested the centre-right would retain power but the stock market has been jittery, with dealers citing rumours of secret polls showing the government's lead narrowing.

The premier said he would overhaul voting procedures at regional and European Parliament level, limit the number of offices which parliamentarians can hold to one other post, and change the constitution to give women better access to politics.
"I am personally in favour of a constitutional measure which would facilitate (women's presence) on a temporaray basis," Juppe said.

An outspoken critic of Juppe within his Gaullist RPR party, National Assembly Speaker Philippe Seguin, launched a last-minute attack on the idea of cohabitation which would inevitably result from a leftist victory.

"The issue in these elections is clear: to allow France to carry all its weight in the negotiations to come by speaking with one voice, a strong voice made legitimate by the French people's vote," Seguin told the daily L'Est Republicain.
"The times are too decisive for a president of the republic to tackle them with a prime minister who fights him for the seat France is entitled to and who contradicts him," he said.

In their last campaign rallies, Juppe urged voters on Thursday to put France back on its feet while Socialist challenger Lionel Jospin battled to defuse charges he could derail a single European currency.
In a final display of strength and unity, heavyweights of the fractious ruling coalition shared a platform in the central city of Lyon with Juppe.
Juppe has said Jospin's conditions and spending would make it impossible for France to meet fiscal targets for a single currency and would cause crisis in the European Union.
Jospin, campaigning in Toulouse in the southwest, reiterated backing for a single European currency on four conditions, including the inclusion of Spain and Italy from the start.

Apart from the inclusion of Italy and Spain, Jospin wants a European "economic government" as a counterweight to the planned EU central bank, a pact of solidarity and growth to combat unemployment and measures to avoid over-valuation of the euro currency.
Jospin urged voters to punish those who had been in power for the past four years and who held "all power" in their hands.
"We mustn't give complete power for five years to a small team which comes from the Paris city hall (where Chirac was mayor)," Jospin told his last big rally.

Socialist president Francois Mitterrand shared power in 1986-88 and 1993-95 with conservative premiers. Chirac called the early elections, partly hoping to work in tandem with an ally for the remaining five years of his seven-year term.

At his last rally in Paris, far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen of the National Front complained he had been kept out of the media spotlight during the campaign. He said earlier that his party may boycott election night broadcasts in protest.
